questions.correctedQuestion: A 42-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is taking weekly methotrexate. Which supplement should routinely be given with methotrexate?
questions.explanation: Folic acid is routinely supplemented with low-dose methotrexate to reduce folate-related adverse effects such as mucositis and cytopenias without substantially reducing efficacy.

optionExplanations.A: Vitamin B6 is not the routine supplement used to reduce methotrexate toxicity.
optionExplanations.B: Folic acid supplementation reduces methotrexate-related folate deficiency and adverse effects.
optionExplanations.C: Vitamin B12 is not the standard routine supplement with methotrexate.
optionExplanations.D: Thiamine is not routinely co-prescribed to prevent methotrexate toxicity.

questions.correctedQuestion: A woman with pneumonia receives amoxicillin and then develops dyspnea, hypotension, and itching. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible?
questions.explanation: Dyspnea, hypotension, and itching occurring rapidly after amoxicillin are characteristic of anaphylaxis, a type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction.

optionExplanations.A: Delayed hypersensitivity is a type IV reaction and is not the typical mechanism of immediate anaphylaxis.
optionExplanations.B: Immediate hypersensitivity is the type I reaction responsible for acute anaphylaxis.
optionExplanations.C: An antigen-antibody complex mechanism describes type III hypersensitivity, not acute anaphylaxis.

questions.correctedQuestion: A woman has malaise and fissures at the angles of her lips. Examination reveals a painless right iliac fossa mass. Which condition or deficiency best explains the presentation?
questions.explanation: The source option appears to refer to Crohn disease/Crohn-related nutritional deficiency. A painless right iliac fossa mass with malaise can occur in Crohn disease, and nutritional deficiencies may cause angular cheilitis. The option wording is unclear.

optionExplanations.A: Alanine deficiency is not a recognized explanation for this presentation.
optionExplanations.B: Folate deficiency can cause mucosal changes but does not explain the right iliac fossa mass as well.
optionExplanations.C: This option is written unclearly as “Cron deficiency anemia”; it appears to intend a Crohn-related condition and is the best available option.
optionExplanations.D: Thiamine deficiency does not explain the characteristic right iliac fossa mass.

questions.originalQuestion:

questions.correctedQuestion: A patient has severe central chest pain radiating to the left shoulder and jaw and has already taken aspirin. What is the next appropriate medication among the options?
questions.explanation: The question appears to refer to older acute coronary syndrome treatment where diamorphine was used for severe pain. Modern ACS care prioritizes urgent ECG/reperfusion assessment and analgesia only when needed; routine opioids are not universally recommended.

optionExplanations.A: Furosemide is not a routine next drug for uncomplicated suspected acute coronary syndrome without pulmonary edema.
optionExplanations.B: Carvedilol is not the immediate next drug simply because the patient has chest pain.
optionExplanations.C: Diamorphine was historically used for severe pain in suspected myocardial infarction, matching the apparent intended answer.
optionExplanations.D: Ramipril is useful in selected ACS patients but is not the immediate analgesic/next step in this presentation.

questions.correctedQuestion: A patient with type 1 diabetes uses basal insulin at night and regular insulin with meals and is fasting for surgery. How should perioperative insulin be managed?
questions.explanation: A patient with type 1 diabetes must not have basal insulin completely omitted. Perioperative insulin is adjusted with glucose monitoring, often using a variable-rate IV insulin regimen for prolonged fasting or major surgery.

optionExplanations.A: Stopping all insulin risks severe hyperglycemia and DKA in type 1 diabetes.
optionExplanations.B: Giving the usual basal dose but omitting all morning management may be unsafe without perioperative glucose monitoring and adjustment.
optionExplanations.C: Giving all insulin exactly as usual while fasting can cause hypoglycemia and is not appropriate for many operations.
optionExplanations.D: A variable perioperative insulin regimen with close glucose monitoring is appropriate, especially for prolonged fasting or major surgery.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.title: Inheritance Risk from a Carrier Grandparent
questions.originalQuestion:
A grandfather is a carrier of cystic fibrosis
Nhat is the risk for his grandson who is 5 year
old?

sourceAnswer.text: Not provided in the source file.

questions.correction: The source does not specify the intervening parent's carrier status or the other biological parent's carrier status. Therefore, the exact risk of an affected grandson cannot be determined from the stem alone.
questions.correctedQuestion: A grandfather is a carrier of cystic fibrosis. What is the risk that his grandson inherits the familial CF variant, assuming the relevant intervening parent and other parent are unaffected/non-carriers as appropriate?
questions.explanation: The question is incomplete because the carrier status of the intervening parent and the other biological parent is not specified. If the intervening parent has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier and then transmits the variant with a 1/2 chance, the grandson's chance of inheriting one CF variant is 1/4; this is not the same as having cystic fibrosis.

optionExplanations.A: A 1/2 risk would apply to transmission from a known carrier parent to a child, not directly from a carrier grandparent.
optionExplanations.B: 1/4 is the implied risk of inheriting the familial CF variant through two successive 1/2 transmission steps, assuming the intervening parent is the carrier pathway.
optionExplanations.C: 1/8 does not follow from the simple two-step transmission calculation.
optionExplanations.D: 1/16 does not follow from the simple two-step transmission calculation.

correctAnswer.text: A — Referral to ophthalmology emergency department for assessment

questions.explanation: A unilateral painful red eye is a potentially sight-threatening presentation. Urgent ophthalmologic assessment is appropriate when serious causes such as keratitis, uveitis, or acute glaucoma are possible.

questions.correction: The source does not provide immediate wound washing as an option and does not specify the source patient's HIV/HBV/HCV status. The best available option is urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis.
questions.correctedQuestion: A general practitioner sustains a needlestick injury while cannulating a patient who injects drugs. What is the most appropriate immediate management among the options?
questions.explanation: The source patient may carry blood-borne viruses, so urgent occupational exposure assessment is required to determine HIV post-exposure prophylaxis and other testing. Immediate wound washing is also essential but is not offered as an option.

optionExplanations.A: Starting HIV treatment without assessment is not the correct approach; post-exposure prophylaxis is different from chronic HIV treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis is the best available option, particularly because HIV PEP is time-sensitive.
optionExplanations.C: Source testing is important but should occur as part of urgent exposure management rather than delaying prophylaxis assessment.
optionExplanations.D: The wound should be washed promptly; deliberately squeezing or encouraging bleeding is not recommended.
